title: Wrong-Way and Right-Way Risk

maps.tested: Reported as two theory questions in a single sitting, with the candidate noting they were 'confusing'. Purely qualitative: identification and example-matching, not calculation.
maps.specifics: Reported verbatim: 'RWR & WWR (2 theory questions): confusing, study...'. The formula card frames it correctly as 'identify if there is any correlation'. WWR = exposure rises as counterparty credit quality falls; RWR = the favourable case. Examinable sub-items: wrong-way collateral, the effect on CCPs, and the modelling approaches (hazard-rate, structural, parametric, jump).

vardeezReading: CR-20: Very Important. "CVA/BCVA and DVA is a favorite topic of GARP. Know the formulas very well. You cannot afford to skip this chapter at all." CR-17: Very Important. "(LO 35.g - Know the terms here very well). LO 35.j This too can be imp. (LO 35.f - This is really imp abt disputes in collateral)"

selectors.name: Classify trades as wrong-way or right-way
selectors.what: Given a trade and a counterparty, say whether it is wrong-way or right-way risk: put options on a stock correlated with the counterparty, FX forwards and cross-currency swaps with a sovereign paid in its local currency, receiver or payer interest rate swaps, commodity swaps hedged by a producer, and CDS where the reference entity is linked to the counterparty (buyer wrong-way, seller right-way).

selectors.name: Test for wrong-way risk
selectors.what: The test itself: wrong-way risk is an unfavourable dependence between exposure and counterparty credit quality, so ask what makes the exposure rise and whether the same event weakens the counterparty; right-way risk is the favourable dependence and reduces CVA. Includes general versus specific WWR, and that WWR increases (not decreases) with counterparty credit quality.

selectors.name: Wrong-way collateral and margin
selectors.what: Which collateral is wrong-way (a government bond securing a payer swap, cash in the currency being paid on a cross-currency swap, an entity's own bonds, a bank's own sovereign bonds) and how collateral affects WWR: margin helps if exposure builds gradually before default and is near useless if exposure jumps at default; it reduces but does not eliminate WWR.

selectors.name: Effect of wrong-way risk on CCPs
selectors.what: Why CCPs are prone to WWR: they rely on variation and initial margin (especially clearing CDSs), initial margin and default fund contributions follow market risk and so implicitly ignore WWR, and the defaulter-pays resources may be insufficient, loading losses on surviving members and possibly the CCP itself.

selectors.name: Wrong-way modelling approaches
selectors.what: Match each approach to its features: hazard rate (intensity) with stochastic spreads, tractable but weak dependence; structural with a bivariate copula, strong effect but opaque correlation; parametric (Hull and White) with a functional link of default probability to exposure; jump, with the FX rate jumping at default, suited to specific WWR.

notSelected: CR-17 e (mechanics and types of collateral) and CR-17 j (market, operational and liquidity risk through collateralisation) carry no A20 shape, no Map point and no Vardeez pointer here; they are drilled in A21, and CR-20 q (implications of central clearing) is not covered beyond the CCP effect in S4.
